paragraphs: The paper addresses how to isolate one speaker from competing sounds using the spatial information available at two ears. Its supervised learning system uses differences in arrival time and intensity between the ears to help identify which parts of a sound mixture belong to the target speaker.

The central representation is a binary mask over time and frequency. An ideal mask retains a small region when the target is stronger there than the interference. For a given spatial arrangement, changing the relative strengths of the sources produces characteristic clusters in the measured spatial cues. A classifier uses this structure to estimate the mask.

Evaluations using signal-to-noise ratio and automatic speech recognition indicate that the estimated masks closely approach the ideal masks. The authors also report significant improvement over an existing approach. Listening results show large intelligibility gains under certain conditions, so the human benefit is conditional rather than established for every listening situation.
neurips-2003-a-classification-based-cock.tldr: A supervised classifier uses two-ear spatial cues to estimate masks that separate a target speaker from interfering sounds.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning in large groups of agents that share a global reward. Three difficulties interact: each agent sees only part of the situation, successful behavior requires coordination, and a shared outcome makes it hard to determine the contribution of an individual action. These are connected problems because an agent must learn from feedback about a world it observes incompletely.

The proposed algorithm models the world from one agent's limited perspective, using a linear system for part of that model. It then uses Kalman filtering to help construct a useful training signal. The emphasis is on making the information available locally support learning, rather than requiring the agent to observe the entire multiagent system.

The authors describe the algorithm as simple and efficient and state that it enables an agent to learn an effective policy. Its contribution connects local modeling, estimation, and feedback construction: the model and filter help turn limited observations into a signal that can guide the agent's choices.
neurips-2003-all-learning-is-local-multi.tldr: A local linear model and Kalman filtering help agents construct useful learning signals in games with shared global rewards.

paragraphs: The paper considers systems in which self-interested agents arrive and leave over time. The designer wants decisions that maximize total long-term value, but agents may benefit from misreporting information. Their strategic choices include claims about when they arrive or depart, as well as how much they value different outcomes.

The approach expresses this online mechanism design problem as a Markov decision process. This connects the sequence of system decisions to a framework for optimizing value over time. The objective therefore accounts for the continuing operation of the system, rather than treating each interaction as a separate decision with only immediate consequences.

The stated result links the solution of that decision process to incentives: when the induced process is solved, its optimal policies can be implemented in a truth-revealing Bayesian-Nash equilibrium. Truthful reporting is thus supported in the specified equilibrium sense. The contribution is the connection between long-term optimization and strategic reporting in a system whose participants change dynamically.
neurips-2003-an-mdp-based-approach-to-on.tldr: Solving an induced Markov decision process can support optimal long-term policies with truthful reporting in Bayesian-Nash equilibrium.

paragraphs: Estimating a person's pose is difficult because appearance varies, scenes contain clutter, and an articulated body has many possible configurations. This paper represents the three-dimensional body as a graphical model. Each limb has variables describing its position and orientation, while conditional probability distributions express relationships between body parts.

Pose estimation becomes a problem of probabilistic inference: evidence about individual parts must be combined with the relationships connecting them. Each limb requires six continuous coordinates. The authors argue that discretizing this space is impractical, so the inference method must handle continuous variables rather than enumerate a fixed collection of limb positions.

The method approximates belief propagation using a generalization of particle filtering. This supplies a way to exchange uncertain information between connected body parts while retaining continuous pose descriptions. The authors state that the framework supports automatic initialization from low-level image cues and is robust to occluded parts and scene clutter. Its importance lies in combining local evidence with a probabilistic model of the assembled body.
neurips-2003-attractive-people-assemblin.tldr: A continuous graphical body model uses approximate belief propagation to assemble human poses from uncertain image evidence.

paragraphs: This paper presents a system that automatically describes people and their activities in video. Its output includes each actor's appearance, the periods when that actor is visible, and a representation of the activity performed during those periods. The system does not require a fixed background, which broadens the video conditions it can address.

The process first tracks people in two dimensions. It then uses an annotated motion capture dataset to synthesize a three-dimensional motion sequence that matches those tracks. This makes motion capture data a bridge between observed image movement and an activity description: the matched motion sequence carries annotations that can describe the video.

The motion capture material is manually labeled beforehand using classes for everyday movement. Those labels can be combined, allowing a description such as jumping while running instead of forcing every action into one exclusive category. Results on videos of real movements are reported as accurate. The automatic video analysis therefore builds on an explicitly prepared, manually annotated motion resource.
neurips-2003-automatic-annotation-of-eve.tldr: The system annotates video activities by matching two-dimensional person tracks to manually annotated three-dimensional motion data.

paragraphs: The paper addresses color constancy through the estimation of image illumination. Its approach uses Bayesian inference and a non-Gaussian probabilistic model of how images are formed. The modeling choice makes the assumed distribution of image formation part of the illumination estimation method, rather than treating that distribution as an incidental detail.

The model's parameters are learned directly from an uncalibrated collection of images. A small additional set of algorithm settings is selected through cross-validation. These are distinct parts of the procedure: the image collection supplies estimates for the probabilistic model, while cross-validation guides the remaining choices needed to run the algorithm.

The authors compare illuminant estimates on publicly available real-world test images using an available code base. They report lower root-mean-square error than the compared color constancy algorithms based on Lambertian surface reflectance. This is an empirical finding on that comparison, supporting the usefulness of the non-Gaussian Bayesian approach for the tested images rather than establishing superiority for all imaging conditions.
neurips-2003-bayesian-color-constancy-wi.tldr: A non-Gaussian Bayesian image model achieves lower illumination-estimation error than the compared methods on real-world test images.

paragraphs: The paper tackles clusters that form long or irregular shapes. Such structures are difficult for methods whose objective favors compact groups. The proposed solution changes the representation first: it transforms the data so that elongated structures become compact, then groups the transformed objects using a compactness-based criterion.

This separation lets the method apply properties of compact clustering to a different geometric problem. The authors state that robustness to outliers transfers through the transformation, producing a method that is highly resistant to outlying objects. The transformation therefore serves both to reveal the desired structures and to make an established type of clustering objective useful for them.

The transformed distances also define a Mercer kernel, which supports a polynomial approximation scheme for the generally NP-hard clustering problem. This is an approximation result, not a claim that exact clustering becomes easy. A further stated advantage is the absence of free kernel parameters, removing that particular source of tuning present in methods such as spectral clustering and mean-shift clustering.
neurips-2003-clustering-with-the-connect.tldr: A connectivity-based transformation makes elongated clusters compact, supporting robust clustering and a polynomial approximation scheme.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover hidden networks from noisy detections of undirected edges. Its motivating example is biological interaction data, where observed connections can include false detections. The task is to infer which edges belong to the underlying graph rather than simply accept the observed network as accurate.

The generative model combines several hidden graphs to produce the observed graph. Each hidden graph has a structural prior based on node degrees, or how many connections nodes have. One hidden graph can represent the network of interest while others represent different noise sources. The combination acts separately on each edge and may be deterministic or stochastic.

The authors call recovery of these constituent graphs untangling; denoising is the special case involving one true graph and independent edge noise. Exact inference is intractable, so they develop an efficient approximation to posterior edge probabilities. These probabilities express uncertainty about whether individual connections exist. The model and algorithm are evaluated on a biological graph inference problem.
neurips-2003-denoising-and-untangling-gr.tldr: Degree-based graph priors and approximate inference estimate which observed edges belong to hidden networks rather than noise.

paragraphs: Eigenvoice adaptation adjusts a speech recognition model to a speaker using a small amount of adaptation data. Standard eigenvoices come from principal component analysis. This paper investigates whether a nonlinear version, specifically kernel PCA, can provide a more effective representation for this adaptation task.

The main obstacle is connecting the kernel representation to the quantities required by the recognizer. Eigenvoices in the transformed feature space must support likelihood calculations in the observation space, both when estimating adaptation weights and during decoding. The authors address this problem by performing kernel PCA with composite kernels, producing their kernel eigenvoice adaptation method.

On the TIDIGITS corpus, the method reduces word error rate by 28–33% relative to a speaker-independent model. In the reported comparison, standard eigenvoice adaptation only matches that model's performance. These results support the proposed nonlinear representation in this evaluation. The contribution combines a way to make kernel eigenvoices usable in recognition with evidence of an adaptation benefit on the stated corpus.
neurips-2003-eigenvoice-speaker-adaptati.tldr: Composite-kernel PCA enables nonlinear eigenvoice adaptation that reduces word error rate by 28–33% on TIDIGITS.

paragraphs: Understanding learning and memory requires reasoning about internal quantities that cannot be observed directly. Connection weights, for example, depend on the history of sensory inputs, actions, and internal dynamics. This makes it difficult to relate observed neural activity or behavior to the hidden state of a learning model.

The paper proposes estimating those hidden quantities from sequences of observable variables. It uses a Bayesian formulation in which a dynamic model connects hidden and observed variables, allowing observations over time to update a posterior distribution over internal quantities. The method applies a particle filter to internal parameters and metaparameters of a reinforcement learning model.

This approach matters because the target is the agent's evolving learning process, not just a summary of its visible behavior. The authors report that they verified the method's effectiveness with artificial data and real animal behavioral data. Those evaluations support using sequential probabilistic estimation to connect observable behavior with otherwise hidden quantities in the specified learning model.
neurips-2003-estimating-internal-variabl.tldr: Particle filtering estimates hidden parameters of a reinforcement learning agent from observable sequences, with tests on artificial and animal data.

paragraphs: Principal components analysis focuses on directions of large variation, while minor components analysis can capture constraints through directions of small variation. Extreme components analysis brings both into one probabilistic model. At its maximum-likelihood solution, the model selects an optimal combination of principal and minor components.

For a fixed number of components, the authors guarantee that the model's log-likelihood is at least as high as that of the probabilistic PCA and MCA models. This is a guarantee about the stated likelihood objective. They also describe an efficient algorithm that reaches the global optimum, making the selection between the two types of components part of a solvable optimization problem.

The shape of the spectrum determines some special cases. For log-convex spectra, the solution uses only principal components; for log-concave spectra, it uses minor components. More general spectra can yield a mixture. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets explore these properties, illustrating why choosing only one end of the spectrum need not always be the best fit.
neurips-2003-extreme-components-analysis.tldr: Extreme components analysis optimally combines principal and minor components under a probabilistic likelihood objective.

paragraphs: The paper models eye movements as decisions that serve ongoing behavior. Its motivation is evidence linking gaze to goal-directed motor actions. Instead of explaining attention only through properties of the visual scene, the model asks which environmental information matters for the task currently being performed.

An eye movement is valuable because it can reduce uncertainty about a task-relevant variable. The model estimates the expected cost of the uncertainty that would remain if a candidate movement were skipped. When several movements are possible, it chooses the one with the highest expected value. This ties the allocation of gaze to the consequences of leaving particular information unresolved.

The authors illustrate the model with a graphical humanoid navigating a sidewalk in a virtual urban environment. Simulations show that the proposed scheduling protocol outperforms a simple round-robin mechanism. That result supports prioritizing gaze according to the estimated cost of uncertainty in the simulated task, providing a concrete demonstration of the model's behavior-driven account of attention.
neurips-2003-eye-movements-for-reward-ma.tldr: A task-driven gaze model chooses eye movements by the expected cost of leaving relevant environmental information uncertain.

paragraphs: The paper proposes clustering genes by separating microarray expression patterns into components associated with biological processes. Its model treats measured expression as the combined effect of independent processes. Linear and nonlinear independent component analysis provide the components used to organize the genes without supervised cluster labels.

Within each component, genes showing significant increases or decreases in expression are grouped together. The authors then test whether each cluster is enriched for particular gene annotations. This connects the statistical grouping to biological interpretation: a functionally coherent cluster should bring together genes whose annotations share meaningful relationships.

Across the evaluated datasets, ICA-based clustering outperforms other leading methods at constructing functionally coherent groups. The authors interpret this as support for the independent-process mixture model of expression. Comparisons among ICA variants show that nonlinear ICA performs best on small datasets, while natural-gradient maximum-likelihood estimation works well across all datasets tested. These are dataset-dependent empirical findings rather than a single universal ranking of the variants.
neurips-2003-ica-based-clustering-of-gen.tldr: ICA separates gene expression into process-related components that yield functionally coherent gene clusters in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: The paper considers clustering data that already comes divided into known groups. The goal is to discover common structure that crosses those existing divisions. A clustering method guided only by the observed features can instead follow the known partition when those features are correlated with group membership.

The proposed information-theoretic approach explicitly incorporates the existing partition. It adds a source of bias that counterbalances feature information when that information aligns with the known groups. The known division therefore helps guide the search toward shared clusters across groups, rather than serving simply as another set of labels to reproduce.

The authors report successful applications to synthetic data and to finding text-based correspondences across religions. The latter application illustrates the intended use: identifying relationships that connect material from different predefined categories. The broader contribution is a clustering framework in which prior knowledge of a partition changes what counts as useful structure, making cross-group commonalities an explicit objective of the analysis.
neurips-2003-identifying-structure-acros.tldr: An information-theoretic clustering method uses known group divisions to uncover common structure that cuts across them.

paragraphs: Projecting a damaged image onto a space of admissible images can change every pixel, even when only a small region is corrupted. This paper proposes identifying the damaged pixels and updating only those pixels. The aim is to make reconstruction selective when noise or an occluding object affects only part of an image.

The method uses an L1 penalty and combines identification and reconstruction in one linear program that can be solved efficiently. A parameterization called the ν-trick lets the user directly specify the fraction of pixels to reconstruct. This gives the reconstruction procedure an interpretable control over how much of the image it changes.

An extension incorporates the knowledge that occlusions often occupy connected blocks, such as sunglasses across a face. It penalizes boundary pixels differently from pixels inside an occluded region. The authors establish the ν-property for this extended formulation as well and report strong experimental results. The contribution is a selective reconstruction method with an additional mechanism for representing spatially grouped damage.
neurips-2003-image-reconstruction-by-lin.tldr: A linear program identifies and repairs corrupted pixels selectively, with an extension for contiguous occlusions.

paragraphs: The paper learns a distance metric from judgments about relative closeness. A training example can state that one object is closer to a second object than to a third, without assigning an exact numerical distance. This makes qualitative comparisons the direct input to learning how objects should be separated.

The method takes a support vector machine approach and expresses the training information as constraints. Those constraints lead to a convex quadratic optimization problem, which the authors solve by adapting standard SVM training methods. The key step is translating an understandable comparison into a mathematical condition on the learned metric.

The authors evaluate the algorithm's performance and modeling flexibility on a collection of text documents. That application examines whether relative comparisons can shape useful distances among documents. The contribution is both representational and computational: it offers a flexible way to state qualitative training information and connects the resulting learning problem to an established family of optimization techniques.
neurips-2003-learning-a-distance-metric-.tldr: Relative closeness judgments become constraints in a convex optimization problem for learning a distance metric.

paragraphs: Spectral clustering uses the eigenstructure of a similarity matrix to divide data into groups. Its intended outcome is high similarity within groups and low similarity across them. This paper develops a cost function that connects a proposed partition to the spectral calculation underlying that division.

The cost measures disagreement between the partition and a solution to the spectral relaxation of a minimum normalized cut problem. Optimizing the same cost with respect to different quantities produces two procedures. Optimizing the partition yields a new clustering algorithm; optimizing the similarity matrix yields a method for learning the similarities themselves.

This shared objective matters because the grouping and its similarity representation can be addressed within one formulation. To make the cost practical to work with, the authors derive a tractable approximation based on the power method for computing eigenvectors. The stated contribution is therefore an objective for both clustering and similarity learning, together with an approximation that makes that objective computationally usable.
neurips-2003-learning-spectral-clusterin.tldr: A shared spectral clustering objective supports both finding partitions and learning the similarity matrix that guides them.

paragraphs: Locality Preserving Projections reduce dimensionality while emphasizing which data points are neighbors. The paper derives linear projection maps by solving an optimization problem designed to preserve that neighborhood structure. This provides an alternative to PCA, whose projection directions are selected for their variance rather than this local relationship objective.

When the high-dimensional observations lie on a lower-dimensional manifold, the authors connect the projections to optimal linear approximations of the manifold's Laplace-Beltrami eigenfunctions. Under that setting, the construction links a linear map to geometry represented by neighborhood relationships. The paper states that LPP consequently shares many representation properties with nonlinear methods such as Laplacian Eigenmaps and Locally Linear Embedding.

A practical distinction is that the resulting map is defined throughout the original ambient space. It can therefore be applied beyond the training points, while retaining its linear form. Illustrative examples on high-dimensional datasets support the proposed approach. The contribution combines a neighborhood-preservation objective with a projection that remains directly applicable to new observations.
neurips-2003-locality-preserving-project.tldr: Locality Preserving Projections produce linear dimensionality reductions that preserve neighborhood structure and apply beyond the training data.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to fit a model linking sensory stimuli to neural spike times. A linear filter first processes the stimulus, and a noisy, leaky integrate-and-fire mechanism then generates spikes. A spike-dependent after-current makes previous spikes relevant to the model, providing a biophysically plausible alternative to memoryless Poisson spiking.

The estimation task is to recover both the stimulus filter and the spiking mechanism's parameters from stimuli and extracellularly recorded spike trains. Although this model had been shown to reproduce various statistics of real neurons, the authors identify parameter estimation as a problem needing closer examination. They formulate it using maximum likelihood.

The central contribution is an algorithm together with a proof that it reaches the global likelihood optimum with reasonable speed. Numerical simulations demonstrate the estimator's effectiveness. The result matters because a more biologically structured spiking model is useful only if it can also be fitted: the paper establishes tractable estimation for the particular stochastic integrate-and-fire formulation it analyzes.
neurips-2003-maximum-likelihood-estimati.tldr: A maximum-likelihood algorithm fits a stochastic integrate-and-fire neuron model with a guarantee of reaching the global optimum.

paragraphs: This paper presents hardware neurons whose continuous-valued behavior is probabilistic. The circuits obtain that behavior by injecting noise into each computing unit. Noise is therefore part of the intended computation: it supplies the randomness needed by the model implemented through the connected neurons.

Interconnecting these units creates a Continuous Restricted Boltzmann Machine. The abstract identifies this model as promising for modeling and classifying noisy biomedical data. The hardware work brings the model's probabilistic units into VLSI circuitry, connecting a statistical learning model to a physical implementation of its computing elements.

The paper also implements the model's minimizing-contrastive-divergence learning algorithm in mixed-mode VLSI. This enables the noisy neurons' parameters to adapt on the chip itself. The contribution covers both the probabilistic behavior of individual units and the machinery for changing their parameters through learning. Together, these elements describe a hardware realization in which stochastic computation and adaptation are both implemented within the circuit system.
neurips-2003-minimising-contrastive-dive.tldr: Noisy VLSI neurons implement a Continuous Restricted Boltzmann Machine with contrastive-divergence learning performed on-chip.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes approximate inference in layered Bayesian networks. In the networks considered, generalized linear models specify the local conditional probabilities. This defines the scope of the analysis while allowing a broad range of probability distributions, including models with discrete variables and models with continuous variables.

The authors examine concentration-of-expectation phenomena and use ideas from large deviation analysis and the delta method to construct inference approximations. These mathematical tools support both the design of the algorithms and the evaluation of their errors. The approximation procedure is therefore tied to an analysis of how accurately it represents the probabilistic calculations of the network.

The resulting class of algorithms is reported to combine very fast computation with superior asymptotic error bounds. The qualification matters: asymptotic bounds describe error behavior in a limiting regime, rather than promising the same error for every individual network. The contribution is an analytically supported route to fast inference across the broad distributional family covered by the stated layered-network formulation.
neurips-2003-on-the-concentration-of-exp.tldr: Concentration analysis yields fast approximate inference algorithms with improved asymptotic error bounds for a class of layered Bayesian networks.

paragraphs: Several methods that use eigendecomposition produce an embedding or clustering only for the points supplied during training. Extending the result to a new point is not straightforward and can otherwise require recomputing eigenvectors. This paper addresses that gap for LLE, Isomap, multidimensional scaling, Laplacian Eigenmaps, and spectral clustering.

The authors provide one framework by interpreting these algorithms as learning eigenfunctions of a kernel that depends on the data. This view turns the spectral result into something that can be evaluated beyond the original training points. It connects methods for dimensionality reduction and clustering through a common account of how their learned structures extend.

Numerical experiments compare extension error with the variability caused by choosing different training data. The reported errors are comparable to that existing variability. This places the approximation in context: applying the learned structure to new examples introduces errors on a scale similar to changes already observed when the underlying embedding algorithms are trained on different data selections.
neurips-2003-out-of-sample-extensions-fo.tldr: A kernel-eigenfunction framework extends several spectral embedding and clustering methods to new points without recomputing their eigenvectors.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether the activity of a recorded neural population can predict the orientation of a visual stimulus. The input consists of spike data from cortical neurons recorded simultaneously. The learning task connects a population's observed activity to a property of the stimulus associated with that activity.

The comparison addresses both sides of the prediction problem. The authors examine different ways to encode the spike data supplied to the learner and different ways to encode the orientation being predicted. This distinguishes the choice of learning algorithm from the choices used to represent its inputs and outputs, making representation an explicit part of the study.

Several kernel algorithms are evaluated using these cortical recordings, and the paper reports their prediction results. Its contribution is a comparative examination of neural decoding in which the algorithm and the coding of the task are considered together. The study therefore asks not only how a learner handles recorded spikes, but also how the form of the prediction problem affects that learning.
neurips-2003-prediction-on-spike-data-us.tldr: The paper compares kernel algorithms and input/output encodings for predicting visual orientation from simultaneously recorded neural spikes.

paragraphs: Many speech-processing methods work with sequences of short-time power spectra. After such a representation is modified, it lacks the phase information needed to reconstruct a time-domain signal with good perceptual quality. This paper focuses on recovering a speech waveform from that phaseless spectrogram.

The authors introduce a generative model connecting speech waveforms with their spectrograms. An efficient optimizer finds the maximum a posteriori waveform given the spectrogram. Instead of alternating between separate phase estimates and spectrally consistent signals, the method infers the waveform directly. This makes phase and spectral consistency parts of a joint optimization.

The paper compares the approach with a standard method using signal-to-noise ratios and supplies audio demonstrations of improved perceptual quality. The stated benefit concerns the reconstructed speech as something listeners hear, alongside its numerical evaluation. The contribution is a probabilistic reconstruction formulation that works directly on the desired signal while accounting jointly for information that phaseless spectral processing leaves unresolved.
neurips-2003-probabilistic-inference-of-.tldr: A generative model reconstructs speech directly from phaseless spectrograms by jointly optimizing the waveform and its implied phase.

paragraphs: The paper addresses color decomposition in histologically stained tissue sections. The task is to separate the spectral contributions present in a stained sample so that they can be analyzed. The authors identify accurate decomposition as an essential part of tissue analysis and diagnosis, making the quality of this separation the central concern.

They present what they describe as the first automated system for performing the decomposition. The title characterizes the approach as unsupervised. The contribution centers on carrying out the separation automatically: the system produces a decomposition of the stained material that can then be assessed against a reference.

The authors compare the system's output with ground-truth data and report favorable results. This evaluates the decomposition itself, rather than merely showing that the automated procedure can run. The reported finding supports the accuracy of the system on the evaluated material. Its relevance to diagnosis comes through the stated importance of reliable spectral decomposition in the analysis of stained tissue sections.
neurips-2003-unsupervised-color-decompos.tldr: An automated, unsupervised system decomposes stained tissue colors and shows favorable agreement with ground-truth data.
